assessment_summary: This paper reports a purposive expert survey (N=51/92 invited) eliciting agreement with 50 proposed AGI-lab safety and governance practices. Strengths include clear scope, preregistration and OSF materials, transparent item/figure reporting, high response rate, and appropriate nonparametric tests with multiple-comparisons correction. Key limitations: (i) small, networked, non-representative sampling (overlap with AGI labs and safety community) risks selection and self-selection bias; (ii) items are abstract, normative, and framed as “should,” inviting acquiescence/social-desirability and inflating agreement; (iii) optional items yield varying n and comparability; (iv) means on ordinal Likert data and across heterogeneous items; (v) limited robustness checks (no nonresponse analysis, alternative phrasings, randomized item order, or weighting); (vi) low power for subgroup tests—null item-level differences are weak evidence; (vii) extrapolation from opinions to “best practices” is not validated by outcomes; (viii) some data withheld for anonymity constrains full replication of subgroup analyses. Overall, the study credibly characterizes preferences within this sample but should avoid generalizing to a broad expert consensus or to practice effectiveness without further evidence.

Strong pantropical mapping, but several methodological and interpretive risks remain. Training data on natural regrowth include substantial omission error in humid biomes; pseudo-absences and misclassification may bias the model. Random forests were trained on class-balanced points and probabilities are treated as calibrated; no prevalence correction or probability calibration is shown, yet expected areas/carbon rely on these values. Validation is not fully spatial; accuracy likely inflated by autocorrelation (declines at greater distances); no formal spatial block cross-validation or predictive uncertainty mapping. Reported “confidence intervals” for total area/carbon are effectively deterministic sums, not uncertainty; overall uncertainty is understated. Predictions at 30 m depend on several coarser predictors (300 m–1 km), so effective map resolution is coarser and may mislead fine-scale planning. Final maps omit socioeconomic predictors (despite similar accuracy), assuming stationarity from 2000–2016 to 2030 and potentially overstating practical feasibility. Carbon estimates exclude permanence/leakage dynamics and use coarse downscaled inputs. Data products are open, but code is only “on request,” limiting full reproducibility.
